query: What minimum sample sizes per stratum and power calculations are needed to support hierarchical SEM, subgroup heterogeneity tests, and mediation with lags?

response.query: What minimum sample sizes per stratum and power calculations are needed to support hierarchical SEM, subgroup heterogeneity tests, and mediation with lags?
response.answer: For hierarchical SEM, subgroup heterogeneity tests, and mediation with lags, a minimum of 200 participants is generally recommended, with more for complex designs. Larger sample sizes improve statistical power and precision.

results.title: Required sample size to detect mediation in 3-level implementation studies | Implementation Science | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Required sample size to detect mediation in 3-level implementation studies | Implementation Science | Springer Nature Link
Statistical tests of mediation are important for advancing implementation science; however, little research has examined the sample sizes needed to detect mediation in 3-level designs (e.g., organization, provider, patient) that are common in implementation research. For 2-sided tests, statistical power to detect mediation was sufficient (≥0.8) in only 463 designs (2.6%) estimated using MVM and 228 designs (1.3%) estimated using MSEM; the minimum number of highest-level units needed to achieve adequate power was 40; the minimum total sample size was 900 observations. While our analysis has important limitations, results suggest many of the 3-level mediation designs that can realistically be conducted in implementation research lack statistical power to detect mediation of highest-level independent variables unless effect sizes are large and 40 or more highest-level units are enrolled. Multilevel mediation analysis is an important tool for testing mechanisms in implementation science; however, little is known about the sample sizes required to adequately power these studies particularly within the range of sample sizes that are feasible for implementation research. We calculated statistical power to detect mediation in 3-level designs (e.g., organization, provider, patient) using a range of plausible input values and sample sizes for implementation research. While some tools have begun to emerge to estimate required sample sizes for 2- and 3-level mediation designs [37, 38], findings from this preliminary research indicate that calculation of statistical power for multilevel mediation is complex and depends on the anticipated range and configuration of study design input values—such as effect sizes and sample sizes—at each level (e.g., organization, clinician, patient). In this study, we address the issue of statistical power and minimum sample sizes required to test mediation in 3-level implementation studies using a generalizable method for calculating statistical power based on Monte Carlo simulations. However, for cell C in Fig. 3 (MVM, 1-sided test), 11 designs (0.1%) had adequate power to detect mediation with level-3 sample sizes of 20 (see Additional file 2). Because statistical power to test mediation in multilevel designs depends on the specific range of input values that are feasible within a given research area, we estimated what sample sizes, effect sizes, and ICCs are required to detect mediation in 3-level implementation research designs.

results.title: Allocation of sample sizes to strata | Sampling Surveys Class Notes
results.content: ## 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. # 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. 1.3 Types of sampling designs. 1.4 Applications of sampling surveys in various fields. 2.3 Sampling units and sampling errors. 3.2 Methods for selecting simple random samples. 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. 4.4 Analysis and estimation in stratified sampling. 5.3 Estimation in cluster sampling. 6.2 Probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling. 6.4 Applications of multistage sampling. 8.1 Sources of sampling errors. 9.1 Factors affecting sample size. 9.2 Sample size calculation methods. 9.3 Power analysis in sampling. Allocating sample sizes to strata is a crucial part of stratified sampling. Proper allocation enhances the overall effectiveness of stratified sampling in producing reliable estimates for the entire population. * Proportional allocation distributes sample sizes proportionally to stratum sizes in the population. * Optimal allocation aims to minimize overall variance for a fixed total sample size. + Allocates more samples to strata with larger variances or sizes. * Neyman allocation optimizes sample allocation considering both stratum size and variability. * Cost-based allocation factors in the cost of sampling units in each stratum. * Power allocation adjusts sample sizes to achieve desired statistical power for hypothesis tests. + Ensures adequate sample sizes for detecting significant differences between strata. + Influences sample allocation in proportional and optimal designs. + Ensures larger strata receive proportionally larger sample sizes. + Higher variance strata often require larger sample sizes for precise estimates. ### Sampling Fraction and Allocation Factor. * Allocation factor determines the relative sample size assigned to each stratum. + Expressed as a ratio or percentage of the total sample size. + Guides the distribution of sample units across strata. ### Sample Size Determination and Precision Requirements. * Sample size determination involves calculating the total number of units to be sampled. + Utilizes formulas specific to the sampling design (simple random, stratified, cluster). + Affects the allocation process by setting the total sample size to be distributed. + Influence sample size calculations and allocation decisions. + Affect sample size determination and allocation decisions. * Sampling efficiency measures the effectiveness of a sampling design in producing precise estimates.
